Let $C_\bullet$ and $D_\bullet$ be chain complexes. A **chain map**
$f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a family of morphisms
$$f_n:C_n\to D_n$$
such that for every $n\in\mathbb Z$,
$$d^D_n\circ f_n=f_{n-1}\circ d^C_n.$$

Equivalently, each square
$$\begin{matrix} C_n&\xrightarrow{f_n}&D_n\\ d^C_n\downarrow&&\downarrow d^D_n\\ C_{n-1}&\xrightarrow{f_{n-1}}&D_{n-1} \end{matrix}$$
commutes.

Let $C_\bullet,D_\bullet$ be chain complexes in an abelian category
$\mathcal A$, and let $f,g:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be chain maps. A **chain homotopy**
$s:f\simeq g$ is a graded morphism of degree $1$,
$$s_n:C_n\to D_{n+1},$$
such that for every $n\in\mathbb Z$,
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n.$$

Equivalently, $f-g$ is the degree-$0$ boundary of the degree-$1$ family $s$ in
[[def-hom-complex-of-chain-complexes]].

A chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ is a **chain homotopy equivalence** if
there exists a chain map $g:D_\bullet\to C_\bullet$ such that
$$g\circ f\simeq1_C,\qquad f\circ g\simeq1_D.$$

Such a map $g$ is called a **homotopy inverse** of $f$.

A left $R$-module $P$ is **projective** if it has the lifting property for epimorphisms: whenever $q:E\to M$ is a surjective module homomorphism and $f:P\to M$ is a module homomorphism, there exists a module homomorphism $\tilde f:P\to E$ such that $q\circ\tilde f=f$ ([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

The lift need not be unique. Projectivity asks for a lift in every such square.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F$ be a function with domain $n$ all of whose
values are nonempty sets. Then the family of its values,
$\mathcal{F} = F[n] = \{\, F(i) : i \in n \,\}$, has a choice function
(Choice function).

This is a theorem of ZF: its proof uses no form of the Axiom of Choice
(The Axiom of Choice).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$. The
natural number $n$ serves as the index set in the von Neumann sense,
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)), so "$F$ has domain $n$"
says precisely that the members of $\mathcal{F}$ are listed as
$F(0), \dots, F(n-1)$. The listing need not be injective, and $\mathcal{F}$ is the
set of values, so repetitions are harmless and are not counted.

The displayed statement and its proof use only a natural-number-indexed
function. They do not identify an arbitrary finite family with a particular
enumeration.

derivations.claim: Put $u=gf$ on $C$. Repeatedly substituting $dh=1-u-hd$ gives, for every integer $s\ge1$, $$dh^s=(-1)^sh^sd+\epsilon_s h^{s-1}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{s-1}(-1)^\ell h^\ell u h^{s-1-\ell},\qquad \epsilon_s=\begin{cases}1&s\text{ odd},\\0&s\text{ even}.\end{cases}$$ For $s=1$ this is the given equation. Multiplying the formula on the right by $h$ and substituting $dh$ in its first term proves the next case: the identity coefficient changes from $\epsilon_s$ to $\epsilon_s+(-1)^s=\epsilon_{s+1}$ and the last summand acquires index $s$. This is finite induction on a specified identity, with no choices.

Define $D_n=\bigoplus_{j=0}^nF_j$ for $n\ge0$, and $D_n=0$ for $n<0$. Define maps $\delta_n:D_n\to D_{n-1}$ by their finite blocks, with column $j$, row $k$, where $0\le j\le n$ and $0\le k\le n-1$: $$ (\delta_n)_{kj}=\begin{cases} 0&j\ge k+2,\\ (-1)^{n+k+1}\partial_j&j=k+1,\\ 1_{F_j}-f_jg_j&j=k,\ n+k\text{ odd},\\ f_jg_j&j=k,\ n+k\text{ even},\\ (-1)^{n+k}f_kh^{k-j}g_j&j<k. \end{cases}$$ All blocks have the displayed source and target, regardless of noncommutativity of $A$. Also define $\alpha_n:C_n\to D_n$ to have only its final component $f_n$, define $\beta_n:D_n\to C_n$ by the row $(h^ng_0,h^{n-1}g_1,\ldots,g_n)$, and let $s_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}$ be inclusion into the first $n+1$ summands. These are specified finite formulas in every degree. We next verify that $D$ is a chain complex and that the named maps have all claimed properties; these are not assumed from a matrix citation.

The final column of $\delta_n$ has only its final block $+\partial_n$. Therefore $\delta_n\alpha_n=\alpha_{n-1}d_n$, using $\partial f=fd$. To check $\beta_{n-1}\delta_n=d_n\beta_n$, consider column $j$. If $j=n$, the assertion is $g_{n-1}\partial_n=d_ng_n$. Otherwise put $t=n-j\ge1$. The superdiagonal contribution is $(-1)^t h^tdg_j$ (zero if $j=0$); the diagonal contribution is $\epsilon_t h^{t-1}g_j-(-1)^{t-1}h^{t-1}ug_j$. Reindexing the lower contributions by $\ell=n-1-k$ gives $-\sum_{\ell=0}^{t-2}(-1)^\ell h^\ell u h^{t-1-\ell}g_j$. The total is exactly $dh^tg_j$ by step 1.1. Thus both intertwining identities hold, without yet assuming $\delta^2=0$.

Directly in the blocks, $$\delta_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}\delta_n=1_{D_n}-\alpha_n\beta_n.$$ Indeed for rows $k<n$ the off-diagonal blocks cancel when $n$ is replaced by $n+1$, and the two diagonal blocks sum to $1$. In row $n$ only the first term is present: its blocks are $-f_nh^{n-j}g_j$ for $j<n$ and $1-f_ng_n$ for $j=n$. They are exactly the final row of $1-\alpha\beta$. For $n=0$ this is simply $\delta_1s_0=1-f_0g_0$. Also $\beta_n\alpha_n=g_nf_n$.

We prove $\delta_{n-1}\delta_n=0$ by induction on $n$. It holds at $n=1$ since $D_{-1}=0$. On the first $n$ summands of $D_n$, identified with $s_{n-1}D_{n-1}$, step 2.2 and the two intertwining identities give $$\begin{aligned} \delta_{n-1}\delta_ns_{n-1} &=\delta_{n-1}(1-\alpha\beta-s_{n-2}\delta_{n-1})\\ &=(1-\alpha\beta)\delta_{n-1}-\delta_{n-1}s_{n-2}\delta_{n-1}\\ &=s_{n-3}\delta_{n-2}\delta_{n-1}=0. \end{aligned}$$ The final equality uses the induction hypothesis, and negative-index terms mean zero. On the remaining summand $F_n$, the two final-column observations give $\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$. Thus the composite vanishes on every summand. This proves $\delta^2=0$. Now step 2.1 says that $\alpha,\beta$ are chain maps, and step 2.2 together with $1-\beta\alpha=dh+hd$ gives a chain homotopy equivalence $C\simeq D$.

Set $T=\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$. For all $n\ge m$, $D_n$ is canonically $T$, because all subsequent summands are zero. For $n\ge m+1$, the square matrix $\delta_n:T\to T$ depends only on the parity of $n$. Write $p$ for its value when $n$ is even. The formulas show that its value when $n$ is odd is $1-p$: the off-diagonal blocks change sign and the diagonal blocks are complementary. Taking two consecutive such degrees in $\delta^2=0$ gives $p(1-p)=0=(1-p)p$, hence $p^2=p$. No assertion that the homotopy idempotent $fg$ itself is strictly idempotent has been made.

Choose the explicit even integer $N=2(m+1)$, and let $q=p:T\to T$. Define $E_n=D_n$ for $0\le n<N$, $E_N=qT\subseteq T=D_N$, and $E_n=0$ otherwise. Restrict $\delta_N$ to $qT$ at the top, and keep $\delta_n$ below it. The square-zero identities remain valid by step 3.1. The maps $J:E\to D$ are the evident inclusions. Define $I:D\to E$ to be identity below $N$, $q$ in degree $N$ and zero above $N$. At degree $N$, $\delta_Nq=\delta_N$ because $1-q=\delta_{N+1}$ and $\delta_N\delta_{N+1}=0$. At degree $N+1$, $q\delta_{N+1}=q(1-q)=0$. These are the only boundary degrees in checking that $I$ is a chain map; $J$ is a chain map by restriction, and $IJ=1_E$.

Define $t_n:D_n\to D_{n+1}$ to be zero for $n<N$ and the canonical identity $T\to T$ for $n\ge N$. Then $$1_D-JI=\delta t+t\delta.$$ Below $N$ both sides are zero. In degree $N$ the right side is $\delta_{N+1}=1-q$, which is the left side. Above $N$ it is the sum of the two complementary matrices $p$ and $1-p$, hence identity, as is the left side. Thus $I,J$ give a specified chain homotopy equivalence between $D$ and the bounded complex $E$.

The modules $E_n$ below $N$ are finite direct sums of the supplied finite free modules, so their concatenated bases are finite. The module $qT$ is generated by the finitely many vectors $q(e_i)$, where $(e_i)$ is that concatenated basis of $T$, and $T=qT\oplus(1-q)T$: write $x=qx+(1-q)x$, and apply $q$ to an element in the intersection to show it is zero. For completeness its projectivity is choice-free. Given a surjection $v:U\to V$ and a right-linear $w:qT\to V$, take, for each of the finitely many $e_i$, a lift in $U$ of $w(qe_i)$. Their simultaneous existence is [F3]. Extend this finite assignment right-linearly to a map $\widetilde w:T\to U$. Then $v\widetilde w=wq$, and restriction to $qT$ is the requested lift. The same proof with $q=1$ gives projectivity of the lower finite free modules. This verifies the actual lifting property, not the general claim that arbitrary free modules are projective in ZF.

Set $a=I\alpha$, $b=\beta J$. These are chain maps and $$1_C-ba=d(h+\beta t\alpha)+(h+\beta t\alpha)d,$$ since $1_C-\beta JI\alpha=(1_C-\beta\alpha)+\beta(1_D-JI)\alpha$. Similarly, using $IJ=1_E$ and step 2.2, $$1_E-ab=\delta_E(IsJ)+(IsJ)\delta_E.$$ Indeed $I(1_D-\alpha\beta)J=1_E-I\alpha\beta J$. These are the explicit required homotopies $H=h+\beta t\alpha$ and $L=IsJ$.

Every degree of $D$, every matrix product used to define its maps, and each component of the homotopies uses a finite sum and finitely many compositions of supplied maps. The single family indexed by all nonnegative degrees is defined by these formulas; it is not obtained by independently selecting a lift or basis in each degree. The only lifts selected in the entire projectivity verification are a finite list for one supplied lifting problem. If the two input complexes vanish below a common integer $b$, reindex $C'_n=C_{n+b}$, $F'_n=F_{n+b}$ with the same differentials and domination equations, apply the construction, and reindex the result back. No infinite recursion of choices and no unbounded-below input is involved. The proof therefore establishes exactly the stated ZF conclusion for the required bounded-below setting.

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on $X$. Its **compactly supported cohomology with local coefficients** is
$$H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)=\varinjlim_{K\subseteq X\text{ compact}}H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L).$$
For compact sets $K\subseteq K'$, the identity is a map of pairs $(X,X\setminus K')\to(X,X\setminus K)$; contravariance gives the displayed system's transition $H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)\to H^k(X,X\setminus K';\mathcal L)$. Thus the coefficient system is always the restriction of one ambient system, and no extension from $X\setminus K$ is being assumed.

Equivalently, an element is represented by $(K,a)$ with $K$ compact and $a\in H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$. Two representatives $(K,a)$ and $(K',a')$ are equal precisely when their images agree for some compact $N\supseteq K\cup K'$. Compact union makes the support poset filtered, so this relation is transitive and addition is performed after transition to $K\cup K'$. This is the same explicit filtered-colimit construction as [[def-compactly-supported-singular-cohomology-of-a-locally-compact-space]], now applied to the relative local-cochain groups.

If $f:X\to Y$ is proper, $\mathcal K$ is a local system on $Y$, and $\theta:f^*\mathcal K\to\mathcal L$ is a coefficient morphism, then each compact $K\subseteq Y$ has compact inverse image and [[prop-local-coefficient-homology-and-cohomology-are-functorial-for-a-map-with-a-coefficient-morphism]] gives
$$H^k(Y,Y\setminus K;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H^k(X,X\setminus f^{-1}K;\mathcal L).$$
These maps commute with enlargement of supports and hence induce the proper pullback $f^*:H_c^k(Y;\mathcal K)\to H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)$. Identity and composite proper maps give identity and composite pullbacks because both assertions already hold before taking the colimit.

When $X$ is compact, $K=X$ is terminal and yields $H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)\cong H^k(X;\mathcal L)$. For $X=\varnothing$, for the zero system, and in negative degrees the group is zero. Local compactness permits the cofinal use of closures of relatively compact open sets exactly as in the published constant-coefficient definition. No simultaneous selection of supports or neighborhoods is made, so the construction is choice-free.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{n+1}(X,A;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Let $M$ be a boundaryless $n$-manifold, $R$ a commutative unital ring, and $K\subseteq M$ compact. There is a unique class
$$[M]^\mathrm{tw}_K\in H_n(M,M\setminus K;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
whose image at every $x\in K$ is the canonical local element: if $o_x$ is
either generator of the integral local group $\mathcal O_x$, it is represented
by a local relative cycle for $o_x$ carrying coefficient $o_x\otimes1_R$.
Equivalently its two typed factors are
$o_x\otimes(o_x\otimes1_R)$, the first in local integral homology and the
second in the stalk $\mathcal O_x^R$. Changing $o_x$ to $-o_x$ changes both
factors and leaves the class fixed. These classes commute with restriction
when the compact support shrinks.

If $M$ is compact with boundary $A$, the boundary orientation system from [[def-orientation-local-system-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]] has a unique relative class
$$[M,A]^\mathrm{tw}\in H_n(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
with these prescribed local images at all interior points. Its pair boundary is the canonical twisted class of $A$ for the outward-normal-first identification $\mathcal O_M^R|_A\cong\mathcal O_A^R$.

Transport along straight radii trivializes $\mathcal L$ with fiber $A=\mathcal L_0$; triangular straight homotopies show that these identifications intertwine every path transport, since the ball is contractible. A contraction induces the usual singular prism homotopy by triangulating each simplex times the interval into its finitely many standard prisms, carrying constant coefficients unchanged. Its boundary identity proves directly that a contractible space has cohomology $A$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees, with no universal-coefficient theorem or chosen primitive family. It also computes homology as $A$ in degree zero and zero elsewhere. For two points the cochain complex splits as two such complexes, so its reduced degree-zero cohomology is $A$ by the difference of the two values.

The same coefficient calculation gives $\widetilde H^k(S^m;A)=A$ for $k=m$ and zero otherwise, for each $m\ge0$. Start with the two-point sphere from step 1.1. For $m\ge1$, cover $S^m$ by the complements of the two poles; both are contractible and their intersection retracts onto $S^{m-1}$. The reduced cohomology Mayer–Vietoris sequence in [F2] identifies each group with the preceding degree on that intersection. This is a finite induction. These identifications are normalized by evaluation on the oriented sphere cycle: split a triangulated sphere into its two oriented hemispheres; the connecting cochain evaluates on their sum as the preceding cochain evaluates on their common boundary. This follows from $(\delta a)(c)=a(\partial c)$ with the difference signs of Mayer–Vietoris. Starting with the oriented difference of the two points, induction proves that evaluation on the oriented fundamental sphere cycle is the resulting isomorphism to $A$, including its sign.

To see the relative comparison on cochains explicitly, extend its small-chain homotopy $D$ to all ambient simplex generators by zero on simplices not contained in this complement. Then $1-\partial D-D\partial$ maps complement chains to their small-chain sum and fixes the sum, while $D$ vanishes on the sum. The resulting quotient maps are inverse up to the displayed chain homotopy; transporting coefficients along the same affine paths gives the identical local-cochain comparison. Restrict to pairs $K\subset U$, $L\subset V$ compact. These unions are cofinal among compact supports in $X$. For any compact $Q\subset X$, choose finitely many relatively compact coordinate neighborhoods whose closures lie in one of $U,V$ and whose interiors cover $Q$. The union of the closures assigned to $U$, intersected with $Q$, is a compact $K\subset U$; the analogous construction gives $L\subset V$, with $Q=K\cup L$. Only one finite cover is selected. 2. A coefficient morphism $\theta:f^*\mathcal K\to\mathcal L$ induces
   $$f^*:H^n(Y,B;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$

At a fixed space, both theories are covariant in coefficient morphisms. These maps preserve identities and composition. If $H:f_0\simeq f_1$ is a homotopy of pair maps, transport along $t\mapsto H(x,t)$ gives $\tau_H:f_0^*\mathcal K\to f_1^*\mathcal K$; the homology maps agree when $\eta_1=\tau_H\eta_0$, and the cohomology maps agree when $\theta_0=\theta_1\tau_H$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $\mathcal L,\mathcal K$ be left $R$-module local systems on $X$. Their **objectwise tensor product** is
$$(\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K)_x=\mathcal L_x\otimes_R\mathcal K_x,\qquad T_\gamma(\ell\otimes k)=T_\gamma\ell\otimes T_\gamma k.$$
The tensor relations make the displayed transport well defined; identity and composition hold on elementary tensors, and $T_{\bar\gamma}\otimes T_{\bar\gamma}$ is its inverse. Thus this is again a local system.

A **local-coefficient pairing** is a natural transformation $b:\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K\to\mathcal N$, equivalently bilinear maps $b_x:\mathcal L_x\times\mathcal K_x\to\mathcal N_x$ satisfying $T_\gamma b_x(\ell,k)=b_y(T_\gamma\ell,T_\gamma k)$ for every path class $\gamma:x\to y$.

For a simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_{p+q}]\to X$, let $\lambda_{0p}^\sigma$ be its affine edge path from $v_0$ to $v_p$. For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and $\psi\in C^q(X;\mathcal K)$ define

The reverse transport is necessary because the back-face value lies over $v_p$ while the output cochain value must lie over $v_0$. The Alexander--Whitney face calculation, with naturality of $b$ on each triangular transport comparison, gives
$$\delta(\varphi\smile_b\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile_b\psi+(-1)^p\varphi\smile_b\delta\psi.$$
Hence cocycles give cup products in cohomology. The same vanishing-on-front-face argument as for ordinary relative cups gives $H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH^q(X,B;\mathcal K)\to H^{p+q}(X,A\cup B;\mathcal N)$ under the usual excisive-triad comparison.

For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and a local chain generator $m\sigma\in C_n(X;\mathcal K)$, define the **cohomology-first cap product** by zero when $p>n$ and otherwise by
$$\varphi\cap_b(m\sigma)=T^{\mathcal N}_{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}\left(b_{v_0}(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),m)\right)\sigma[p,\ldots,n].$$
Here forward transport is necessary because the retained back face begins at $v_p$. The published front/back face cancellation, with the same naturality squares, yields
$$\partial(\varphi\cap_b c)=(-1)^p\left(\varphi\cap_b\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap_b c\right).$$
Consequently cap descends to the same relative quotient patterns as [[def-relative-cap-product]], with the chain coefficient system changed from $\mathcal K$ to $\mathcal N$ in the target. In particular,
$$H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;\mathcal N),$$
and
$$H^p(X;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X,A;\mathcal N).$$

If a cohomology class is represented with compact support $K$, cup with any ordinary class remains supported in $K$, while the cap of a class in $H^p(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$ with a class in $H_n(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal K)$ is an absolute class. Empty spaces, zero systems or rings, $p=0$, $p=n$, and $p>n$ follow from the displayed formulas. Only finite faces of a supplied simplex occur, so no AC is used.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on $X$. Its **compactly supported cohomology with local coefficients** is
$$H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)=\varinjlim_{K\subseteq X\text{ compact}}H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L).$$
For compact sets $K\subseteq K'$, the identity is a map of pairs $(X,X\setminus K')\to(X,X\setminus K)$; contravariance gives the displayed system's transition $H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)\to H^k(X,X\setminus K';\mathcal L)$. Thus the coefficient system is always the restriction of one ambient system, and no extension from $X\setminus K$ is being assumed.

Equivalently, an element is represented by $(K,a)$ with $K$ compact and $a\in H^k(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$. Two representatives $(K,a)$ and $(K',a')$ are equal precisely when their images agree for some compact $N\supseteq K\cup K'$. If $f:X\to Y$ is proper, $\mathcal K$ is a local system on $Y$, and $\theta:f^*\mathcal K\to\mathcal L$ is a coefficient morphism, then each compact $K\subseteq Y$ has compact inverse image and [[prop-local-coefficient-homology-and-cohomology-are-functorial-for-a-map-with-a-coefficient-morphism]] gives
$$H^k(Y,Y\setminus K;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H^k(X,X\setminus f^{-1}K;\mathcal L).$$
These maps commute with enlargement of supports and hence induce the proper pullback $f^*:H_c^k(Y;\mathcal K)\to H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)$. Identity and composite proper maps give identity and composite pullbacks because both assertions already hold before taking the colimit.

When $X$ is compact, $K=X$ is terminal and yields $H_c^k(X;\mathcal L)\cong H^k(X;\mathcal L)$. For $X=\varnothing$, for the zero system, and in negative degrees the group is zero. Local compactness permits the cofinal use of closures of relatively compact open sets exactly as in the published constant-coefficient definition. No simultaneous selection of supports or neighborhoods is made, so the construction is choice-free.

Let
$$\cdots \to A_{n-1} \to A_n \to A_{n+1} \to A_{n+2} \to A_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
and
$$\cdots \to B_{n-1} \to B_n \to B_{n+1} \to B_{n+2} \to B_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
be long exact sequences in an abelian category, together with a morphism of
these sequences. If the four comparison maps at $A_{n-1},A_n,A_{n+2},A_{n+3}$
are isomorphisms, then the comparison map $A_{n+1} \to B_{n+1}$ is an
isomorphism.

derivations.claim: If $A$ is empty, both maps are [F2]'s compact duality, so assume it is nonempty. Put $N=W\setminus A$, $C_d=c(A\times[0,d))$ and $K_d=W\setminus C_d$ for $0<d<1/2$. Every compact $L\subset N$ lies in some $K_d$: intersect it with the closed compact collar segment of height at most $1/2$; on the nonempty intersection the continuous height has a positive minimum since $L$ misses $A$. Choose $d$ below that minimum; if the intersection is empty any sufficiently small $d$ works. Compactness supplies a finite atlas of $W$ by ordinary and half-space charts. Restricting these charts to $N$ gives a finite atlas by open Euclidean subsets. Thus [F2]'s finite-atlas duality applies to $N$. Pushing the collar inward with the function $t\mapsto t+\varepsilon\chi(t)$, where $\chi=1$ near zero and vanishes before height $1/2$ and $\varepsilon>0$ is small enough, gives a homotopy inverse to $N\hookrightarrow W$. Linear interpolation of this push gives the homotopies, stays inside the collar, and restricts to positive heights on $N$.

Excision identifies its domain with $H^p(N,N\setminus K_d;\mathcal L|_N)$. These maps commute with decreasing $d$. The cofinality of the $K_d$ from step 1.1 and the representative definition of the support colimit therefore give a canonical isomorphism $H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_c^p(N;\mathcal L|_N)$. To verify independence, move two representatives to a common smaller collar core; the natural relative maps and common-support equality identify them there. This selects representatives for a single class only.

By [F1], the image of $z$ in $H_n(W,C_d;\mathbb Z)$ is the excision image of the support orientation class of $N$ at $K_d$. A relative cocycle on $(W,C_d)$ vanishes on $C_d$. Cap with two chains representing this equality differs by a boundary and by a cap term supported in $C_d$; the latter is zero. The cap boundary formula [F4] turns the former difference into a target boundary. Thus under step 2.1 the relative cap map on $W$ is exactly compact-support cap on $N$ followed by inclusion $N\hookrightarrow W$. Both maps are isomorphisms by step 1.1 and [F2], proving $H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L)$.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on an arbitrary space $X$. For a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$, write $v_i=\sigma(e_i)$ and $\gamma_{01}^\sigma(t)=\sigma(1-t,t,0,\ldots,0)$.

The **intrinsic singular local chain group** is
$$C_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\bigoplus_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0}.$$
Write an element of the $\sigma$-summand as $m\sigma$. Its boundary is
$$\partial(m\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}(m)(\sigma\delta_0)+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^im(\sigma\delta_i),$$
and the boundary of a zero-simplex is zero. The exceptional zeroth face transports its coefficient from the old first vertex $v_0$ to the new first vertex $v_1$; all other faces keep $v_0$.

The **intrinsic singular local cochain group** is the product
$$C^n_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)=\prod_{\sigma:\Delta^n\to X}\mathcal L_{v_0},$$
so a cochain $\varphi$ assigns $\varphi(\sigma)\in\mathcal L_{v_0}$ to every simplex, with no finite-support requirement. Its positive coboundary, consistent with [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]], is
$$(\delta\varphi)(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_{01}^\sigma}^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(\sigma\delta_0)\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\delta_i).$$
Now the exceptional face value is transported back from $v_1$ to $v_0$.

For $A\subseteq X$, restrict $\mathcal L$ along the inclusion and set
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)/C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L),\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)=\ker\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X;\mathcal L)\to C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(A;\mathcal L)\bigr).$$

For a connected CW complex with chosen basepoint $x$, universal cover $\widetilde X$, $\pi=\pi_1(X,x)$, and base fiber $M=\mathcal L_x$ carrying $g m=T_{\bar g}m$, the equivalent universal-cover models are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
The first tensor product is the balanced construction of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] using the right action of [[def-right-group-ring-action-on-the-chains-of-a-universal-cover]]. For the second, convert that right chain module to a left one by
$$g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}.$$
Thus an equivariant cochain has the correctly typed rule
$$\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c),$$
not a module-Hom between one right and one left module.

The intrinsic/tensor identification sends $\widetilde\sigma\otimes m$ to the simplex $\sigma=p\widetilde\sigma$ with coefficient obtained by transporting $m$ along the path represented by $\widetilde\sigma(e_0)$. If $\widetilde\sigma$ is replaced by $\widetilde\sigma\cdot g$, that path is changed by the loop $g^{-1}$ and the coefficient becomes the transport of $gm$, exactly the balanced relation. The analogous statement for cochains proves the displayed equivariance rule. These maps respect the two boundary formulas term by term.

The **cellular local chain and cochain groups** of a connected CW complex are
$$C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R)\otimes_{R[\pi]}M,\qquad C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X;\mathcal L)=\operatorname{Hom}_{R[\pi]}\bigl({}_{R[\pi]}C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(\widetilde X;R),M\bigr).$$
For a CW pair, quotient by the lifted subcomplex before tensoring and use the corresponding relative cellular complex before applying equivariant Hom. For a disconnected CW complex, take the direct sum of chain complexes and the degreewise product of cochain complexes over its components. Universal-cover coordinates of this componentwise description require a supplied basepoint in each component; the intrinsic complexes require no simultaneous basepoint choice and remain the definition when no such family is supplied.

The next lemma proves square-zero and independence of supplied lift bases. Empty spaces and negative degrees give zero groups, the zero local system gives the zero complexes, and constant systems reduce to the ordinary formulas because every transport is the identity.

derivations.claim: For a singular simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_n]\to M$, put its coefficient in $\mathcal R_{\sigma(v_0)}$ and take the direct sum of those right modules over all singular simplices. For $n\ge1$ define $d(c\sigma)=T_{01}(c)\,\sigma[1,\ldots,n]+\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^i c\,\sigma[0,\ldots,\widehat i,\ldots,n]$, and let the degree-zero differential be zero. Every face map is right-linear because transport is, so this defines right-$R$ linear differentials without assuming that $R$ is commutative. To check $d^2=0$, pair the two terms deleting vertices $i<j$. Their signs are $(-1)^{i+j-1}$ and $(-1)^{i+j}$. If $i>0$, both coefficients are $c$. If $i=0<1<j$, both coefficients are $T_{01}(c)$. If $(i,j)=(0,1)$, the coefficients are $T_{12}T_{01}(c)$ and $T_{02}(c)$, which agree because the two-edge path is endpoint-fixed homotopic to the direct edge in the simplex and transport is a groupoid functor. Thus every pair cancels. This includes degenerate simplices and degree one, where the next differential is zero. These are the underlying abelian local chains of [F1], now equipped with their verified right-$R$ structure.

Choose a finite cover by coordinate balls $U_1,\ldots,U_m$ with charts onto convex Euclidean balls, including a ball centered at $o$. This uses compactness and only a finite selection. Their intersection graph is connected: otherwise the unions belonging to different graph components would be disjoint nonempty open sets partitioning connected $M$. For each edge choose one point in the intersection, a finite selection; join it to each chart center by its straight coordinate segment. Choose a spanning tree by the finite index order and concatenate these segments to get paths from $o$ to every chart center. For $x\in M$, take the least-index chart containing it and follow its center path by the straight segment to $x$; at $o$ use the constant path. Denote this explicitly prescribed path by $\gamma_x$. This defines paths for all points from one finite list of charts and edge points, rather than selecting an infinite family of paths.

Transport the supplied basis $1\in\mathcal R_o$ along $\gamma_x$ to obtain a basis at each $x$. Thus [F1] makes every $C_j$ the free right $R$-module on its actual singular $j$-simplices. Write $e_x$ for the degree-zero basis and $e_\sigma$ for the degree-one basis of a path $\sigma:x\to y$. The degree-one boundary is $d_1e_\sigma=e_y g_\sigma-e_x$, where $g_\sigma\in H$ is the transition unit obtained by transporting first along $\gamma_x$, then along $\sigma$, and back along $\gamma_y$. For $x\ne o$, the path $\gamma_x$ is itself one singular one-simplex; denote its basis element by $p_x$. These basis elements are distinct because their terminal points are distinct, and $d_1p_x=e_x-e_o$. Put $p_o=0$.

Change the degree-zero basis to $e_o$ and $b_x=e_x-e_o$ for $x\ne o$. This is invertible even with infinitely many vertices: the inverse is $e_x=b_x+e_o$, and every vector has finite support. Retain the degree-one basis elements $p_x$. For every other one-simplex $\sigma:x\to y$, replace its basis element by $q_\sigma=e_\sigma-p_y g_\sigma+p_x$. This is another invertible basis change, with inverse $e_\sigma=q_\sigma+p_y g_\sigma-p_x$. Direct substitution gives $d_1q_\sigma=e_o(g_\sigma-1)$, whereas $d_1p_x=b_x$.

Let $Q_1$ be free on the $p_x$, $Q_0$ free on the $b_x$, and $Q_j=0$ in other degrees, with differential $p_x\mapsto b_x$. Let $C'_1$ be free on the remaining $q_\sigma$, $C'_0=Re_o$, and $C'_j=C_j$ for $j\ge2$. The differential of a degree-two chain has zero $p_x$ coefficient for every $x$: applying $d_1$ would otherwise give a nonzero corresponding $b_x$ coefficient, contrary to $d_1d_2=0$ proved in step 1.1. Thus $d_2$ lands in $C'_1$, and higher differentials already stay in $C'$. This proves the claimed direct sum of complexes. Its contractible summand has the explicit homotopy $b_x\mapsto p_x$, zero on all other degrees. Dualizing this actual homotopy gives the cochain equivalences for any coefficient module; no exactness assertion about an infinite product or choice of primitives is needed.

The image of $d'_1$ is the right ideal generated by the elements $g_\sigma-1$. All transition units belong to $H$, so this ideal is contained in $\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R$. Conversely every $h\in H$ is realized by transport along a based loop at $o$. That loop is one singular one-simplex and is not one of the removed $p_x$, whose endpoints differ. Its reduced boundary is $e_o(h-1)$. Thus every generator of the displayed ideal occurs, and equality follows.

If $H=\langle t\rangle$ is cyclic, $t^k-1$ is a right multiple of $t-1$ for every integer $k$: use the finite geometric sum for $k>0$, zero for $k=0$, and $t^{-k}-1=-t^{-k}(t^k-1)$ for negative powers. Since powers of $t$ commute with $t-1$, this last expression is also a right multiple. The ideal is therefore $(t-1)R$, including $H=\{1\}$ with zero ideal. The other two sufficient conditions for principality are literal. All basis changes and homotopies were explicit finite-support formulas, and the only initial choices were finite. This proves the stated choice scope.

Restriction induces an isomorphism $$H^2(Y,T;\mathcal R^\vee)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^2(W,A\cup D;\mathcal R^\vee).$$ To see the actual excision condition, remove from $X$ a closed core outside a short open collar of its seam $A$. That core is closed in $Y$ and lies in $\operatorname{int}_Y T$, because it misses the seam. Excision [F2] then leaves $W$ together with that short seam collar, and the remaining relative subspace is $D$ together with the collar. Pushing the collar to $A$ is a homotopy equivalence of pairs with $(W,A\cup D)$. Coefficient transports along the collar give its local-system comparison. This proves the isomorphism; it is restriction and commutes with forgetting relative conditions.

Let $u_p\in H^2(W,\partial W;\mathcal R^\vee)$ be the dual of $\bar p$, and let $v_p$ be its inverse image under step 1.1. Map $v_p$ into $H^2(Y,\partial Y;\mathcal R^\vee)$ since $\partial Y\subset T$. Its cap with $[Y,\partial Y]$ is $\overline{i_*p}$. Indeed the image of the orientation class in the excised pair restricts to $[W,\partial W]$, since their pointwise orientation images on the interior of $W$ agree. The support/relative cap comparison of [F2] therefore identifies the cap with $u_p$ on $W$, followed by inclusion in $Y$. On representatives one may first apply the image-preserving small-chain operator: the portion in $X$ caps to zero because $v_p$ vanishes on $T$, and the portion on the remaining collar core gives precisely the cap on $W$. Changes of the orientation representatives are a boundary plus a chain in the relative subspace; the cap boundary identity makes their caps a boundary plus zero. Thus this is the actual cap map, not an unsupported geometric push of cycles.

Relative duality [F1] now says that the class in step 2.1 is the relative dual of $\overline{i_*p}$. Its absolute cohomology image restricts to the absolute image of $u_p$ on $W$, by the last sentence of step 1.1. Naturality of evaluation gives $$\lambda_Y(i_*p,i_*q)=\langle j_Yv_p,i_*q\rangle=\langle i^*j_Yv_p,q\rangle=\langle j_Wu_p,q\rangle=\lambda_W(p,q).$$ Here each cochain system uses the restriction of the same ambient parallel Hermitian form, so no unrestricted frame change or independent coefficient identification is being inserted.

The displayed equality immediately preserves any finite list of zero self-pairings and unit dual-pairings. Every collar core and representative comparison is chosen for one finite calculation, and the small-chain operators are fixed formulas. derivations.claim: First construct a compatible metric from finite data. Compactness supplies finitely many coordinate balls $V_i$ whose closures lie in larger coordinate balls with charts $\varphi_i$; take their coordinate images concentric balls of radii $r_i<R_i$. A continuous radial function $\chi_i$ equals one on $\overline V_i$, decreases linearly to zero before the larger chart boundary, and is zero elsewhere on $M$. The finitely many functions $\chi_i$ and $\chi_i\varphi_i$, extended by zero, are continuous because their coordinate supports are compactly contained in the charts. Their combined map $F$ into a finite Euclidean space is injective: for $x$, choose $i$ with $x\in V_i$, so $\chi_i(x)=1$; equality $F(x)=F(y)$ forces $\chi_i(y)=1$ and $\varphi_i(x)=\varphi_i(y)$, hence $x=y$. A continuous injection of a compact space into a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image: images of closed subsets are compact and hence closed. Therefore $d(x,y)=|F(x)-F(y)|$ is a compatible metric. All choices so far are finite.

Choose a finite cover of $M$ by contractible coordinate balls. It has a positive Lebesgue number $\lambda$: for a finite open cover the functions $x\mapsto d(x,M\setminus U)$, with the empty-complement case assigned a positive constant, are continuous; their finite maximum is everywhere positive and has a positive minimum on compact $M$. A sufficiently small number below that minimum makes every set of diameter less than $\lambda$ lie in some member, by taking a point in the set and using the corresponding distance bound. Choose $0<\epsilon<\lambda/10$. There is a finite cover by smaller coordinate balls $B_j$ of $d$-diameter less than $\epsilon$, because one can shrink a coordinate neighborhood inside a metric ball of radius less than $\epsilon/2$ and then take a finite subcover. Choose $0<\delta<\epsilon$ that is a Lebesgue number for this second finite cover. Any pair of points of distance less than $\delta$ can therefore be joined inside one $B_j$ by its straight coordinate path, of diameter less than $\epsilon$.

Compactness gives a finite $\delta/4$-net of anchors $a_0=o,a_1,\ldots,a_s$, with the basepoint added first. For each unordered distinct anchor pair of distance less than $\delta$, put an edge in a finite graph and map it to the straight coordinate path in the least-index $B_j$ containing that pair; the reverse orientation uses the reversed path. Map each vertex to its anchor. For any $x\in M$, let $a(x)$ be the least-index anchor at distance less than $\delta/4$. Join $x$ to $a(x)$ by the straight path in the least-index $B_j$ containing them. These connectors have diameter less than $\epsilon$ and are defined by finite lists and the chart formulas, without choosing a family of paths. At $o$ take the constant connector.

Let $\ell$ be any based loop in $M$. Uniform continuity on its compact interval gives a finite subdivision such that each segment has image diameter less than $\delta/4$. Write its successive endpoints as $x_i$ and anchors as $a_i=a(x_i)$. Then $d(a_i,a_{i+1})<3\delta/4$, so the selected graph has an edge between successive distinct anchors; repeated anchors give the constant path. The loop formed by this edge, the original loop segment and the two endpoint connectors is contained in a set of diameter less than $4\epsilon$: each connector and edge has diameter less than $\epsilon$, and its initial or terminal point lies within $\delta/4$ of an endpoint of the original short segment. This entire small loop therefore lies in one of the contractible coordinate balls of step 2.1. Contract it there. Gluing these finitely many homotopies, with adjacent connectors cancelling, shows that $\ell$ is based homotopic to the resulting graph edge loop at $a_0=o$. Thus the fundamental-group map of the component of this finite graph containing $a_0$ is onto.

Choose a spanning tree of that finite graph component by its finite vertex order. For every oriented edge outside the tree, follow the tree path from the base vertex to its initial vertex, traverse the edge, and return along the tree path from its terminal vertex. These finitely many loops generate all graph edge loops: insert the corresponding tree paths at successive vertices of an edge loop; the intervening inverse tree paths cancel, and a tree-edge loop contracts by deleting immediate reversals. Step 4.1 then makes their images generate $\pi_1(M,o)$. All graph data, covers, nets and tree paths were finite; a loop uses its own one finite subdivision and finite homotopy construction. No infinite family of generators, partitions or primitives was selected. This proves the statement without AC.

Let $L$ be a finite geometric simplicial complex with an ordered vertex set, and let $\mathcal R$ be a local system of rank-one free right modules over an arbitrary unital ring $R$. Its finite simplicial chain complex $F_*(L;\mathcal R)$ and intrinsic singular chain complex $C_*(L;\mathcal R)$ admit $R$-linear chain maps
$$P:C_*(L;\mathcal R)\to F_*(L;\mathcal R),\qquad J:F_*(L;\mathcal R)\to C_*(L;\mathcal R)$$
with $PJ=1$ and an explicitly constructed chain homotopy $JP\simeq1$. Choices of bases at its finitely many vertices make $F_*$ bounded finite-free.

Consequently, for every compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, and every such local system supplied with a base-fiber identification with $R$, its nonnegative singular chain complex is free with a formula-specified basis and is $R$-linearly chain-homotopy dominated by a bounded finite-free complex. No choice principle, triangulation of $M$, or assertion of finite CW type for $M$ is assumed.

Work in ZF. Let $A$ be any associative unital ring and let $C$ be a chain complex of unital right $A$-modules with $C_n=0$ for $n<0$. Supply a chain complex $F$ with $F_n=0$ outside $0\le n\le m$, each $F_n$ supplied as a finite free right $A$-module, chain maps $f:C\to F$ and $g:F\to C$, and right $A$-linear maps $h_n:C_n\to C_{n+1}$ such that
$$1_C-gf=d_Ch+hd_C.$$
Then there is a chain complex $E$ of finitely generated projective right $A$-modules, zero outside $0\le n\le N$ for some finite $N$, together with explicitly constructed chain maps $a:C\to E$, $b:E\to C$ and chain homotopies
$$1_C-ba=dH+Hd,\qquad 1_E-ab=dL+Ld.$$
The modules of $E$ below its top degree can be taken finite free, and its top module is the image of an explicit idempotent on $\bigoplus_{j=0}^mF_j$.

Neither freeness nor projectivity nor finite generation of the modules of $C$ is required. Thus the result applies in particular to the nonnegative singular or cellular free chain complexes with specified bases. More generally it applies after reindexing whenever $C$ and $F$ have a common finite lower bound. It makes no assertion for inputs unbounded below and no assertion that $E$ is finite free or that any underlying space has finite CW type. No form of the Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $W$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold with boundary $A$ and a supplied boundary collar $c:A\times[0,1)\to W$. Let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with the integral relative orientation class $z=[W,A]$ gives isomorphisms in every integer degree:
$$H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L),\qquad H^p(W;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L).$$
The maps commute with every coefficient action commuting with transport, including noncommutative ring actions on the underlying abelian-group systems. No choice principle, smoothness, triangulation or finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented boundaryless Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with its integral orientation class induces isomorphisms
$$H^p(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;\mathcal L)$$
for every integer $p$, without a choice principle. The maps respect any coefficient-ring action commuting with transport, and in particular apply to local systems of modules over a noncommutative ring by forgetting to abelian groups and retaining that action. No smoothness, triangulation or prescribed finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

Assume AC. Let $G$ be a discrete group, let $A=\mathcal N G\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(G))$ have its canonical faithful normal trace $\tau$, and give matrices the unnormalized trace $\tau_r((a_{ij}))=\sum_{i=1}^r\tau(a_{ii})$. For a projection $p\in M_r(A)$ put $\dim_A(pA^r)=\tau_r(p)$; for any right $A$-module take the supremum of dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules. These dimensions are independent of the projective representation. If $L\subseteq pA^r$ is any submodule and $q$ is the projection onto its Hilbert closure in $p\ell^2(G)^r$, then $q\in M_r(A)$, $q\le p$, and
$$\dim_A L=\tau_r(q),\qquad \dim_A(pA^r/L)=\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q).$$
In particular a Hilbert-dense submodule has dimension-zero quotient. Modules of dimension zero are closed under submodules, quotients, extensions and filtered colimits. For any matrix $B\in M_{r,s}(A)$, its kernel and Hilbert-closed image are projection modules, its algebraic image is isomorphic to its support projection module, and
$$\tau_s(P_{\ker B})+\tau_r(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=s.$$

Work under the standing AC convention for finite von Neumann modules. Let $A=\mathcal N G$ with its finite trace, and let all Hilbert modules below be ranges of projections on finite sums of $\ell^2(G)$. For a bounded self-adjoint module operator $J$ define its positive and negative inertia by the traces of $\mathbf1_{(0,\infty)}(J)$ and $\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0)}(J)$, and its signature by their difference. Each inertia is the supremum of dimensions of closed module subspaces on which the form $\langle Jx,x\rangle$ is strictly positive or strictly negative, respectively. If $T:H_0\to H_1$ is bounded, injective and has dense image, then $T^*JT$ and $J$ have the same inertia. If $J$ is invertible, $V\subseteq H$ is closed, and $V^{\perp_J}\subseteq V$, then the form on $H$ and its restriction to $V$ have equal signatures. Kernels contribute zero. These statements include ordinary real signatures by complexification and the trivial-group trace.

Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with supplied boundary collar, and let $R$ be an involutive unital ring. Supply a based rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$, a base-fiber identification with $R$, unitary monodromy and its parallel standard Hermitian form. For $p\in H_2(W;\mathcal R)$ let $a_p\in H^2(W,\partial W;\mathcal R^\vee)$ be the inverse cap-duality image of $\bar p$, using the form to identify the intrinsic dual system with $\overline{\mathcal R}$. Define
$$\lambda(p,q)=\langle j(a_p),q\rangle,$$
where $j$ forgets the relative condition and the last pairing is intrinsic cochain evaluation. Then
$$\lambda(p,q)=\overline{\lambda(q,p)}$$
for all $p,q$. In particular $\lambda(\ell_i,d_j)=\delta_{ij}$ implies $\lambda(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. No choice axiom, triangulation or geometric transversality of surfaces in dimension four is required.

Let $W,X$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds with supplied boundary collars and decompositions $\partial W=A\sqcup D$, $\partial X=A\sqcup B$. Glue their copies of $A$ by a supplied orientation-reversing identification, obtaining $Y=W\cup_A X$ with $\partial Y=D\sqcup B$. Supply one ambient rank-one right-$R$ local system on $Y$, where $R$ is an involutive unital ring. On each connected component supply a base-fiber identification with $R$ and unitary monodromy, and use its transported standard Hermitian form. Use its restrictions and the induced orientations on $W,X$.

For the intersection pairings defined by inverse relative cap duality, passage to absolute cohomology and evaluation,
$$\lambda_Y(i_*p,i_*q)=\lambda_W(p,q)\qquad(p,q\in H_2(W;R)).$$
In particular all isotropic and dual-pair identities for homology classes in $W$ persist under their inclusion in $Y$. The result applies to topological manifolds and requires no geometric surface transversality or choice principle.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_{n-1}(A;\mathcal L|_A)\to\cdots$$
and
$$\cdots\to H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(A;\mathcal L|_A)\xrightarrow{\delta}H^{n+1}(X,A;\mathcal L)\to\cdots.$$
The homology connector sends a relative cycle represented by $c$ to $[\partial c]$. The cohomology connector sends a cocycle $a$ on $A$ to $[\delta\widetilde a]$, where $\widetilde a$ is its extension by zero to simplices not contained in $A$. Naturality uses the variances of the preceding functoriality proposition.

Let $M$ be a boundaryless $n$-manifold, $R$ a commutative unital ring, and $K\subseteq M$ compact. There is a unique class
$$[M]^\mathrm{tw}_K\in H_n(M,M\setminus K;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
whose image at every $x\in K$ is the canonical local element: if $o_x$ is
either generator of the integral local group $\mathcal O_x$, it is represented
by a local relative cycle for $o_x$ carrying coefficient $o_x\otimes1_R$.
Equivalently its two typed factors are
$o_x\otimes(o_x\otimes1_R)$, the first in local integral homology and the
second in the stalk $\mathcal O_x^R$. Changing $o_x$ to $-o_x$ changes both
factors and leaves the class fixed. These classes commute with restriction
when the compact support shrinks.

If $M$ is compact with boundary $A$, the boundary orientation system from [[def-orientation-local-system-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]] has a unique relative class
$$[M,A]^\mathrm{tw}\in H_n(M,A;\mathcal O_M^R)$$
with these prescribed local images at all interior points. Its pair boundary is the canonical twisted class of $A$ for the outward-normal-first identification $\mathcal O_M^R|_A\cong\mathcal O_A^R$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $\mathcal L,\mathcal K$ be left $R$-module local systems on $X$. Their **objectwise tensor product** is
$$(\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K)_x=\mathcal L_x\otimes_R\mathcal K_x,\qquad T_\gamma(\ell\otimes k)=T_\gamma\ell\otimes T_\gamma k.$$
The tensor relations make the displayed transport well defined; identity and composition hold on elementary tensors, and $T_{\bar\gamma}\otimes T_{\bar\gamma}$ is its inverse. Thus this is again a local system.

A **local-coefficient pairing** is a natural transformation $b:\mathcal L\otimes_R\mathcal K\to\mathcal N$, equivalently bilinear maps $b_x:\mathcal L_x\times\mathcal K_x\to\mathcal N_x$ satisfying $T_\gamma b_x(\ell,k)=b_y(T_\gamma\ell,T_\gamma k)$ for every path class $\gamma:x\to y$.

For a simplex $\sigma:[v_0,\ldots,v_{p+q}]\to X$, let $\lambda_{0p}^\sigma$ be its affine edge path from $v_0$ to $v_p$. For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and $\psi\in C^q(X;\mathcal K)$ define
$$(\varphi\smile_b\psi)(\sigma)=b_{v_0}\left(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),T^{\mathcal K}_{\overline{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}}\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\right).$$
The reverse transport is necessary because the back-face value lies over $v_p$ while the output cochain value must lie over $v_0$. The Alexander--Whitney face calculation, with naturality of $b$ on each triangular transport comparison, gives
$$\delta(\varphi\smile_b\psi)=\delta\varphi\smile_b\psi+(-1)^p\varphi\smile_b\delta\psi.$$
Hence cocycles give cup products in cohomology. The same vanishing-on-front-face argument as for ordinary relative cups gives $H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH^q(X,B;\mathcal K)\to H^{p+q}(X,A\cup B;\mathcal N)$ under the usual excisive-triad comparison.

For $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathcal L)$ and a local chain generator $m\sigma\in C_n(X;\mathcal K)$, define the **cohomology-first cap product** by zero when $p>n$ and otherwise by
$$\varphi\cap_b(m\sigma)=T^{\mathcal N}_{\lambda_{0p}^\sigma}\left(b_{v_0}(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]),m)\right)\sigma[p,\ldots,n].$$
Here forward transport is necessary because the retained back face begins at $v_p$. The published front/back face cancellation, with the same naturality squares, yields
$$\partial(\varphi\cap_b c)=(-1)^p\left(\varphi\cap_b\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap_b c\right).$$
Consequently cap descends to the same relative quotient patterns as [[def-relative-cap-product]], with the chain coefficient system changed from $\mathcal K$ to $\mathcal N$ in the target. In particular,
$$H^p(X,A;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;\mathcal N),$$
and
$$H^p(X;\mathcal L)\otimes_RH_n(X,A;\mathcal K)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X,A;\mathcal N).$$

If a cohomology class is represented with compact support $K$, cup with any ordinary class remains supported in $K$, while the cap of a class in $H^p(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal L)$ with a class in $H_n(X,X\setminus K;\mathcal K)$ is an absolute class. Enlargement of $K$ commutes with the formulas, giving the compact-support cup and supportwise cap operations used in duality. Constant systems and multiplication recover the published operations. Empty spaces, zero systems or rings, $p=0$, $p=n$, and $p>n$ follow from the displayed formulas. Only finite faces of a supplied simplex occur, so no AC is used.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold and $o\in M$. There is a finite based graph mapped continuously into $M$ such that its induced fundamental-group map is onto. Consequently $\pi_1(M,o)$ has a finite generating list, without a choice principle. No triangulation or smooth structure on $M$ is assumed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] over $R$ to each of the finitely many compact manifolds in a proposed finite diagram, obtaining $C(M;R)\simeq E(M)$ with bounded finite-projective $E$, actual chain maps $a:C\to E$, $b:E\to C$, and actual homotopies for $ba\simeq1_C$, $ab\simeq1_E$. Realize each projective term as $eR^r$ for a supplied finite idempotent $e$, using [F1]'s explicit presentation. Its conjugate right dual is $e^*R^r$, after the finite dual-coordinate identification. Every map or homotopy between two such finite projective terms is a finite rectangular matrix: compose it with the source idempotent and include its target in the ambient finite free module. This assertion includes dual maps; it does not identify the dual of an infinite singular direct sum with a direct sum.

For an inclusion $u:C(B)\to C(M)$ use the finite model map $u_E=a_Mub_B$ and its mapping cone, with differential $d(y,x)=(d_My+u_Ex,-d_Bx)$. This cone is bounded finite-projective and compares to the actual singular cone. For example a comparison to the singular cone is $(y,x)\mapsto(b_My-H_Mub_Bx,b_Bx)$ when $1-b_Ma_M=dH_M+H_Md$: substituting gives a chain map because $ub_B-b_Mu_E=d(H_Mub_B)+(H_Mub_B)d$. Its component maps induce homology isomorphisms, so the cone comparison is a homology isomorphism by the exact mapping-cone sequence. For the pair, the singular inclusion is a split injection in every degree, using the actual subset of singular generators lying in $B$. The map from its cone to the quotient $C(M,B)$ is a homology isomorphism, with kernel the contracted cone of the identity of $C(B)$. Under [A1] the comparison cones are chain contractible: a bounded-below acyclic complex of projectives splits first onto its lowest term, leaving a projective kernel, and then recursively onto that kernel. Free singular terms are projective here by choosing preimages of their basis elements using AC. Thus these are actual chain homotopy comparisons, not just homology identifications.

The same construction applies to a finite gluing graph of embedded compact pieces whose distinct seams join different pieces and are disjoint closed whole boundary components. Take collar-enlarged open neighborhoods $U_v$ of the pieces with no triple intersections and their disjoint seam overlaps $U_e$. The small singular chain sequence is $$0\to\bigoplus_e C(U_e)\to\bigoplus_v C(U_v)\to C^{\mathrm{sm}}(X)\to0.$$ Its first map is the two inclusions with opposite signs. It is degreewise split by assigning a small simplex to the least piece containing it; a duplicated simplex is exactly in one seam overlap. The supplied collar deformations retract $U_v$ onto $M_v$ and $U_e$ onto $N_e$, with their actual coefficient comparisons; the displayed exact sequence is the open-neighborhood sequence before those homotopy replacements. Small subdivision and its homotopy [F5] compare the last term with all singular chains. Taking finite models and the finite matrix of signed inclusion maps therefore gives a bounded finite-projective cone model for the entire diagram, by step 2.1. Dualizing these actual chain homotopy comparisons gives cochain comparisons too. The first-vertex free bases identify the scalar-extended singular complex literally with the singular complex of the extended $A$ fiber. Tensoring with $A$ preserves the comparisons because their homotopy identities are actual identities, requiring no flatness assumption. On finite projectives the dual coefficient comparison is $\overline{\operatorname{Hom}_R(E,R)}\otimes_R A\cong\overline{\operatorname{Hom}_R(E,A)}$, verified directly on the idempotent coordinates; thus no infinite product is interchanged with tensor.

Transfer cap with one finite relative fundamental representative $z$ using these chain comparisons. The absolute cochain cap lands in relative chains, and relative cochain cap lands in absolute chains. They are chain maps with the cap signs of [F5]: in the chain reindexing of a degree-$p$ dual cochain use differential $(-1)^{p+1}\delta$, so $\partial(\bar\alpha\cap z)=(-1)^{p+1}\overline{\delta\alpha}\cap z$ after the appropriate relative quotient. Conjugate the intrinsic left duals to right modules via [F2]. For example the absolute-to-relative map on finite models is the composite of the dual of $a_M$, cap with $z$, and the relative comparison back to $E(M,\partial M)$. Its induced homology is an isomorphism by [F2] and steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. Both ends are bounded finite-projective, so its mapping cone is bounded acyclic finite-projective and is contractible: split its lowest term and continue through only finitely many degrees. All resulting maps and homotopies are finite matrices over $R$. This proves a finite-projective cap chain homotopy equivalence, before any Hilbert completion.

Each finite $R$ matrix acts boundedly on finite sums of $\ell^2(G)$, with norm bounded by the finite sums of absolute values of its group coefficients. An idempotent $e$ has closed Hilbert range, since it is the kernel of $1-e$; its orthogonal range projection $p$ lies in a matrix algebra over $A$ by [F3]. The identities $ep=p$, $pe=e$ give $eA^r=pA^r$. Hence the finite projective complexes and all cap maps and their inverses and homotopies from step 4.1 complete to bounded Hilbert-module chain maps. Bounded homotopies send closures of boundaries into closures of boundaries and induce inverse maps on completed reduced homology. Thus completed cap duality is a bounded isomorphism, without a closed-range assertion for any differential.

In a completed degree term $p\ell^2(G)^r$, let $p_Z$ project onto $\ker d_i$ and $p_B$ onto $\overline{\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}}$. These are matrix projections in $A$, $p_B\le p_Z\le p$, and the algebraic matrix kernel is exactly $p_ZA^r$: check columns for one inclusion and use $d_ip_Z=0$ for the other. Harmonic projection gives an algebraic homology surjection onto $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^r$ with kernel $p_BA^r/\operatorname{im}d_{i+1}$, of dimension zero by [F3]. Inclusion of harmonic algebraic cycles splits that surjection. The map $P_i\to(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^r$, sending each operator column to its value on $\delta_e$, is injective: an operator annihilating $\delta_e$ annihilates all its right translates. Its image is dense because group-ring columns are Hilbert dense. This gives exactly the algebraic/projective/completed dictionary in the Statement, with no false surjectivity onto the completed Hilbert module.

All pair and finite-graph homology and cohomology sequences from step 3.1 are algebraically exact after tensoring with $A$: their finite cone sequences are degreewise split and their actual comparisons are homotopy equivalences. Their maps on harmonic parts are bounded, since inclusions, cone connectors and degreewise projections are finite matrices followed by orthogonal harmonic projections. Write each algebraic term as $P\oplus T$ as in step 6.1. Every map $T\to P'$ is zero, since its image is zero-dimensional whereas every nonzero vector in a finite projection module generates a positive-dimensional submodule by [F3]. For consecutive maps $f,g$, let $K_A=\ker g_P$, a finite algebraic projection module whose Hilbert closure is the kernel $K_H$ of the completed map. Lift $K_A$ as harmonic algebraic cycles into the middle homology. Its actual $g$ image lies in the target $T'$, so $K_A/\ker(g|_{K_A})$ is zero-dimensional. The quotient formula [F3] makes that kernel dense in $K_H$. Algebraic exactness puts it in the actual preceding image; projecting a preimage off its $T$ part does not change its harmonic image. Thus $\operatorname{im}f_P$ contains this dense kernel and is contained in $K_A$. The closure of the completed preceding image is precisely $K_H$. This proves weak exactness, and proves only weak exactness, without assuming images closed.

Riesz duality of the completed finite projective complex identifies its completed reduced cohomology with the Hilbert dual of completed reduced homology: conjugate adjoint differentials have harmonic space the orthogonal complement of their boundary closures. Compose inverse relative cap, restriction, and this identification to obtain the bounded middle intersection operator $J_M$. The cochain cap/evaluation definition agrees on algebraic $A$ homology by step 3.1 and the same simplex formula, and [F4] makes its extension Hermitian. Thus $J_M$ is self-adjoint. Its Hilbert radical is exactly $\ker J_M$, a closed projection submodule. Removing that radical leaves its orthogonal complement, but its restricted operator need not be bounded below; signature is defined by the positive and negative spectral projections, which discard only the zero spectral projection. If $M$ is closed, restriction has no relative condition, so cap duality from step 5.1 and Riesz duality make $J_M$ boundedly invertible. This is the only place below where invertibility is asserted.

The cap boundary, restriction and support/excision identities persist in these completed models. Restriction and cone connectors are finite matrix maps by steps 1.1 and 3.1, and the actual cap equivalences are finite matrices by step 4.1. For the identities needed here, work directly on singular cochains with the $A$ coefficient fiber: [F2,F5] give the cap-boundary identities on the finite orientation chain, and [F4] gives the support/excision identities, with the prescribed standard form. Step 3.1 identifies this actual cohomology and homology with the finite $A$ complexes, so the identities hold on their harmonic algebraic parts. These are dense by step 6.1 and all the maps just named are bounded by step 5.1, hence the identities hold on the Hilbert completions. No assertion that an arbitrary homology identity supplies a chain homotopy is needed. A change of finite-projective model is handled by the finite chain maps $a'b$ and their actual comparison homotopies; they induce bounded inverse harmonic maps. Both models compute the same singular $A$ cap/evaluation form, so these harmonic maps preserve it on the dense algebraic parts and then everywhere. Inertia is invariant under this bounded congruence by [F3], proving model independence.

Let $X$ now be a closed oriented four-manifold decomposed into a finite graph of compact topological pieces with disjoint closed seams as in step 3.1. Put $H=\mathscr H_2(X)$ and let $j:\bigoplus_v\mathscr H_2(M_v)\to H$ sum the actual inclusions, with $U=\overline{\operatorname{im}j}$. Its closed intersection operator $J_X$ is invertible by step 7.2. Under cap and Riesz duality, $U^{\perp_{J_X}}$ is the kernel of cohomology restriction from $X$ to the pieces, since evaluation on a piece is pairing with its inclusion. Weak graph Mayer–Vietoris exactness from step 7.1 identifies this kernel with the closure of the connecting image from $\bigoplus_e\mathscr H^1(N_e)$. The cap boundary identity of step 8.1 identifies its dual image, up to the fixed seam orientation signs, with the closure of the inclusion image from $\bigoplus_e\mathscr H_2(N_e)$. Cap is boundedly invertible on $X$ and on each closed three-dimensional seam, so these are actual equal closed submodules. Each seam inclusion factors through a piece, hence that image lies in $U$. Therefore $U^{\perp_{J_X}}\subseteq U$, establishing coisotropy with image closures retained throughout.

The pullback form $j^*J_Xj$ is the orthogonal sum of the pieces' relative intersection forms. Same-piece terms are [F4]'s actual collared inclusion identity. For a cross term, take a piece's inverse relative-cap class. Excision identifies it with a class on $X$ relative to the union of the other pieces: remove their closed cores off the seams and retract the remaining collars, exactly as in [F4]'s support comparison. Its cap is the inclusion image of the original piece's class by the local orientation identity. Its restriction to every other piece is zero, so its evaluation on every other piece's class is zero. This proves cross-term vanishing by relative cochains, without a geometric transverse-intersection assertion. Apply the same argument directly with $A$ coefficient fibers; steps 6.1 and 8.1 extend it continuously to the completed harmonic modules. Orientation reversal negates inverse cap and hence the corresponding piece operator.

Discard $\ker j$, a null summand of $j^*J_Xj$. On its Hilbert orthogonal complement, $j$ is injective with dense image in $U$, without any assertion that this image is closed. Dense congruence in [F3] identifies the pullback signature with the signature of $J_X|_U$. Coisotropic reduction in [F3] and step 9.1 identify this last signature with the signature on all of $H$. Step 10.1 and finite additivity of spectral trace therefore prove $$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)=\sum_v\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(M_v).$$ The boundary piece operators may have nonclosed ranges and radicals; the argument uses invertibility only for the closed $J_X$, and their zero spectral projections contribute zero.

For the stated possibly partial-boundary gluing $W=W_0\cup_NW_1$, take its closed double $X=W\cup_{\partial W}(-W)$. Extend the coefficient system by the fold map $X\to W$. The reflection swapping the two copies reverses orientation and preserves the folded system, so bounded cap naturality and model independence give $\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)=-\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(X)$, hence zero. View the same $X$ as the finite graph of pieces $W_0,W_1,-W$, with seams $N$ and the remaining boundary components of $W_0,W_1$. These seams are disjoint closed whole components, with no triple intersections. Step 11.1 gives $0=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1)-\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W)$, the required formula. Empty remaining boundary or disconnected pieces produce a finite disjoint union of the same constructions; empty seams give ordinary direct sums. Apply the identical proof to the trivial coefficient group to obtain ordinary complex signature additivity; complexification of a finite real symmetric form preserves both inertia dimensions, giving the ordinary real formula.

Finally take a possibly uncountable target $G$. Include the glued manifolds and their doubles among the finitely many spaces considered. A component with boundary is a retract of its closed double by the collar fold map, so its fundamental group is a quotient of that closed double's group. Thus [F6], applied to closed compact components, makes all the needed fundamental groups finitely generated, so the subgroup $H$ generated by the images of those finitely many generating lists is countable; enumerate its elements by finite words and take the first word for each element. Construct the entire finite-projective diagram first over $\mathbb CH$ and extend its finite matrices to $\mathbb CG$. For each right coset $H\gamma$, its subspace $\ell^2(H\gamma)$ is invariant for every left-$H$ matrix; the unitary $\delta_h\mapsto\delta_{h\gamma}$ identifies the restriction with the same $\ell^2(H)$ matrix. Kernel, closure, harmonic and positive/negative spectral projections are therefore the identical operators on these blocks, by functional calculus. Their canonical trace is the sum of identity-coordinate diagonals, so the $G$ trace equals the $H$ trace on every relevant projection, regardless of the number of cosets. This proves the stated dimension and signature equality and compatibility with the countable convention. Full AC was the standing Hilbert and projective-comparison hypothesis; all completed maps were finite matrices, and no smoothing, finite CW inference, ordinary-versus-$L^2$ closed index equality or analytic rho foundation entered the proof.
